title: CJI in Hyderabad: AI detectors wrongly flag 3 in 5 non-native essays

slides.head: CJI in Hyderabad: AI detectors wrongly flag 3 in 5 non-native essays
What happened
slides.body: Opening the two-day CLEA conference, the CJI said banning AI tools would be neither practical nor wise, and colleges need clear rules on how students may use them.

slides.head: Why it matters
slides.body: He cited a study finding widely used detectors wrongly marked more than three in five essays by non-native English speakers as machine-written.

slides.head: Essays wrongly flagged as AI
slides.body: He also proposed making legal aid work compulsory for every law student before graduation.

slides.head: Dig deeper
slides.body: This is the first international edition of the CLEA conference, held in Hyderabad.

slides.head: What to watch
slides.body: Whether CLEA drafts model guidelines on disclosing AI use in legal research. Ask: Do Hyderabad colleges tell students which AI detector they use and how it is checked?

slides.head: Spill the tea, daily
slides.body: Hyderabad news in 30 seconds, with the numbers and the questions. Follow for tomorrow's drop: spillthetea.news

captions.instagram:
CJI in Hyderabad: AI detectors wrongly flag 3 in 5 non-native essays

Chief Justice of India Surya Kant told a Commonwealth legal education conference in Hyderabad that no student should be held guilty of misconduct on a machine's word alone.

Why it matters: He cited a study finding widely used detectors wrongly marked more than three in five essays by non-native English speakers as machine-written.

Source: Times of India. Image: Times of India
